pages.text: Avoid foreclosure | USAGov Skip to main content Avoid foreclosure Foreclosure happens when a lender seizes and sells a property because the homeowner does not pay the mortgage. Learn what to do if your home is at risk of foreclosure. Important Ads and websites may offer to help you save your house from foreclosure but ask for money upfront. These may be scams. Avoid and report mortgage relief scams. What happens when you do not pay your mortgage When you buy a home or other type of property and do not pay the mortgage, the lender can start the foreclosure process. This is when a lender repossesses a property and sells it. Learn more about how the foreclosure process works. Communicate with your lender As soon as you know that you are going to have trouble paying your mortgage: Contact your lender immediately and let them know you are having financial difficulties. This gives your lender time to work with you to create a financial plan. Do not stop paying your bills. Seek help early. Do not wait until you cannot make payments before you act. Learn how to talk to your lender if you have trouble paying your mortgage. Get help from housing counselors and programs Government programs and housing counselors can help you learn about your options as you work to keep your home. Close b-jazz Mapper since: May 07, 2017 Last map edit: November 16, 2026 My Story One of things I like to do when meeting new mappers is ask them how they discovered and started contributing to OSM. Well my story goes back to the very, very early days of OSM. I heard about it through some forums (I don’t even remember which) and took a look at it. To say that the tools were in their infancy would be an understatement. There were no aerial images to make use of, things were mostly done through GPS tracks. Living in the heart of Silicon Valley, there were already some roads mapped out. There were areas right where I lived that were definitely wrong, but the tools just weren’t there for me to invest time, so I walked away for several years. Many years later, I was doing some geocaching in my spare time and there was a big stink when geocaching.com moved from Google maps to OSM. At the time, I didn’t get why they would do that. (A while later it became painfully obvious as I realized that Google was charging through the nose for high traffic users of their services.) I didn’t really pick up OSM at that time either. Add another year or two and I saw that Strava had switched from Google to OSM as well and I really started to be more aware that OSM was becoming more and more mainstream. When I retired in 2017, I wanted to have a project to work on so I started learning OSM and finding more and more ways to contribute. Close b-jazz's Diary Cleaning up Golf Courses in the United States Posted by b-jazz on 3 November 2026 in English . Last updated on 4 November 2026. Written 2025-10-30… Published 2026-11-03 About three years ago, during my day-to-day mapping activities, I came across a golf course that had some obvious errors. I didn’t think much of it at the time. Just a fairway that was drawn right across the top of a green. But the more golf courses I looked at, the more frequently I encountered this error. I soon learned about a golf course simulator video game that was built on OpenStreetMap data and was attracting a large influx of simulator enthusiasts who weren’t seasoned OSM mappers. Along with that came various tools to aid in converting OSM data into these simulators, as well as tutorial videos that made some very bad assumptions about how golf courses should be mapped. These factors set the stage for some very bad mapping practices to spread around the world. My understanding is that attempts were made to correct these bad habits at the source, but the tutorial author wasn’t interested in revising or removing his video. Combine that with YouTube’s bad decision to hide down votes on videos, and you’re left with de facto training material that is widely disliked but that new golf course mappers have no way of knowing is a poor source of truth. pages.text: Bangladesh: Wage protests force hundreds of garment factories to close Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close 3 November 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Mukimul Ahsan , BBC Bangla and Koh Ewe Garment workers in Bangladesh stage protests to demand higher wages Hundreds of garment factories in Bangladesh have been forced to close after days-long protests by workers demanding higher wages. On Sunday, protests in the capital Dhaka turned violent with protesters blocking roads, vandalising factories and setting vehicles on fire. They also clashed with police, who fired tear gas to disperse them. Police later said that dozens of protesters had been arrested. Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242; £180), more than double the current standard, citing rising costs of living. Bangladesh's textile industry employs around four million workers and manufactures garments for major global brands including H&M, Primark and Uniqlo. There are fears in the industry that the prolonged unrest could disrupt production and affect international buyers, state news agency BSS reported. The garment industry generates nearly $40bn every year for Bangladesh, accounting for around 10% of its GDP. Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton stepped forward with a plan to establish a national bank—which still stands in Independence National Historical Park—that would give the federal government more authority to handle the fiscal situation. His proposal incited a debate that tested the US Constitution’s boundaries and laid the foundation for the country’s financial system. Photograph: Khalil Hamra/AP Greenhouse gas emissions Barbados PM urges global citizens to demand methane cuts at Cop31 summit Mia Mottley launches petition to reduce powerful greenhouse gas emissions as UN climate meeting enters second week Fiona Harvey in Antalya Mon 16 Nov 2026 00.00 EST Last modified on Tue 17 Nov 2026 00.09 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Staying silent on the climate crisis is pushing the world closer to disaster, the prime minister of Barbados , Mia Mottley, has said, urging people around the world to force a confrontation with politicians who are failing to do what is needed. Taking action on methane emissions could be the emergency brake that gives the world time to decarbonise, Mottley said. She is urging people to sign a global petition to cut the powerful greenhouse gas . She hopes to gather 1.5bn responses to her petition , in an echo of the 1.5C temperature limit countries have pledged to protect. “We have to let them know the good news: that if we can control methane, we can reduce temperature [rises] by 0.3C to 0.5C ,” she said during an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit

NPS Comprised of 2.7 million acres on the Seward Peninsula in northwest Alaska, Bering Land Bridge is one of the nation's most remote national park units. Established by the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) on December 2, 1980, the preserve aims to protect a landscape that contains an invaluable record of flora and fauna, the history of human migration between Asia and North America and supports an ongoing tradition of subsistence culture. An opportunity to travel to a land visited by so few can provide solitude and beauty not often available in others parts of the country. Proper planning and equipment is needed for a successful trip as its remote nature makes it difficult to call for help and can take several hours to reach medical facilities. Cleanup activities take place at active and abandoned waste sites, federal facilities and properties, and where any storage tanks have leaked. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school. "Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says. One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village. "They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says. Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married. "It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains. Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home. Once they enter the any colony, the beetles can never leave. Sceptobius beetles are seen grooming an ant as part of their evolved symbiotic relationship. D. Miller, Parker Lab/Caltech By Jason Bittel Published February 5, 2026 Life may look like a paradise for beetles living in ant colonies. Plump, wriggling ant larvae and helpless eggs sit waiting to be devoured, while hundreds of thousands of ants stand at the ready to ward off predators and parasites. There’s just one catch for these beetles, revealed in a new study published in the journal Cell . If one leaves the ant colony, it’ll be dead in less than a day. From bacteria living inside insect guts to mycorrhizal fungi on plant roots, symbiotic organisms abound across the tree of life, says Joseph Parker , an evolutionary biologist at the California Institute of Technology and senior author of the study. All these symbiotes have something in common that can also be a liability—their evolutionary entwinement has progressed so far, they can no longer live without their hosts. Parker and his colleagues wanted to know why. They tackled this question by investigating the odd relationship between a rove beetle known as Sceptobius lativentris and its host, the velvety tree ant. pages.text: Before Mountain Biking Became One of the Most Popular Recreational Sports, Adventurous Souls of the American West Had to Invent a Rugged Bike Skip to main content Breeze’s earlier conceptual drawing for the Breezer 1 prototype. In the 1960s and ’70s, a countercultural movement drew a new generation of pioneers to the West. Suddenly, ski bums, scofflaws, draft dodgers and hippie homesteaders were joining the miners and hardscrabble farmers of mountain towns like Crested Butte, Colorado. Looking for a way to navigate both the Pontiac-bedeviling potholes in town as well as the dirt roads leading into the mountains, a small crew of Crested Butte transplants began building handmade off-road-ready bikes. They used a hodgepodge of vintage parts, in particular from World War II-era Schwinn bicycles. The group called itself the Grubstake Gang (named after a favorite watering hole), and they rejoiced when their heavy cruisers, outfitted with fat tires, proved capable of handling the punishing unpaved roads into and out of town. In September 1976, 15 cyclists attempted a seemingly impossible feat: riding these “klunkers” over 12,700-foot Pearl Pass to Aspen. The next day, just two riders rolled into Aspen; the steep Colorado stones of the 38-mile road had destroyed all the other klunkers. Around the same time, a group of teenagers in California’s Marin County—they called themselves the Larkspur Canyon Gang —were tinkering and racing their own garage-built bikes down the steep roads of Mount Tamalpais , north of San Francisco. pages.text: Ben Franklin Wasn’t Serious When He Implied the Wild Turkey Would Be a ‘Respectable’ National Symbol … but He Wasn’t Wrong, Either Skip to main content The head of a male turkey is distinguished by the colorful dewlap and caruncles on its neck. Joanna Lentini The wild turkey is a noble beast: the muscular, bronze-sheened ancestor of the barnyard turkeys we eat today. While the two technically belong to the same species, the barnyard variety is relatively new on the scene. People began domesticating wild turkeys in what is now Mexico more than 2,000 years ago, selectively breeding them over generations to become fat and docile. Wild turkeys, meanwhile, have inhabited North America for a much longer time—hundreds of thousands of years. Hunters still eat them, of course, and appreciate the lean gaminess of the wild flesh. But for most of us, the bird is less about sustenance than about a glimpse of the true national temperament: resourceful and restless, by turns noble and idiotic—as liable to swagger into view as to bolt for the trees.
